name: PGM1-CDG (phosphoglucomutase 1)
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type It

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A mixed disorder of glycosylation and glycogen metabolism caused by deficiency of phosphoglucomutase 1, which interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate
A distinctive clinical clue is a bifid uvula or cleft palate combined with exercise intolerance, myopathy and rhabdomyolysis with raised creatine kinase
Hypoglycaemia (often ketotic or with fasting), hepatopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy and short stature are recognised features
It is one of the treatable CDGs: oral galactose supplementation improves the glycosylation defect and several clinical and biochemical markers
Transferrin analysis characteristically shows a mixed type I and type II pattern, reflecting both reduced site occupancy and abnormal galactosylation
Endocrine abnormalities including hypogonadotrophic features and thyroid changes can occur
Management combines dietary galactose supplementation with attention to hypoglycaemia, cardiac and muscle complications; diagnosis is confirmed by PGM1 testing
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphoglucomutase 1 interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, a step central both to glycogen turnover and to producing the UDP-glucose and UDP-galactose needed for glycosylation. Deficiency simultaneously impairs glycogen handling, causing exercise intolerance and hypoglycaemia, and depletes nucleotide sugars, causing under-glycosylation with abnormal galactosylation. This dual mechanism gives the characteristic mixed type I/type II transferrin pattern. Supplying galactose replenishes UDP-galactose, bypassing part of the block and improving glycosylation, which is why the disorder is treatable.
additionalDifferentials: Glycogen storage disorders with exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis (e.g. McArdle disease)
Other CDGs, particularly those with a mixed transferrin pattern
Fatty acid oxidation disorders presenting with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and myopathy
Isolated cleft palate or bifid uvula syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a mixed type I/type II pattern
PGM1 molecular genetic testing and enzyme assay
Serum creatine kinase, particularly during exercise or rhabdomyolysis
Fasting and provocation studies to characterise hypoglycaemia
Liver function tests, endocrine screen and growth assessment
redFlags: Hypoglycaemia, especially with fasting or intercurrent illness
Rhabdomyolysis or acute muscle injury with exertion
Signs of heart failure from dilated cardiomyopathy
reference.prognosis: With galactose supplementation and careful management of hypoglycaemia and cardiac disease, many patients do well, though dilated cardiomyopathy can be a serious complication; overall outlook is more favourable than most severe CDGs given the available treatment.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by overlooking the cleft palate or bifid uvula clue
Not recognising PGM1-CDG as galactose-responsive and withholding treatment
Attributing exercise intolerance solely to a primary glycogenosis
Failing to screen for and monitor dilated cardiomyopathy
references: Scriver's OMMBID, congenital disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, disorders of glycosylation and glycogen metabolism
management: Oral D-galactose supplementation to replenish UDP-galactose and improve glycosylation and biochemical markers
Avoidance of prolonged fasting with regular complex-carbohydrate intake to prevent ketotic and fasting hypoglycaemia
Prevention and treatment of exertional rhabdomyolysis through activity modification and hydration, with monitoring of creatine kinase
Cardiac surveillance with serial echocardiography for dilated cardiomyopathy and standard heart-failure therapy if it develops
Monitoring and treatment of hepatopathy, endocrine dysfunction including hypogonadotrophic and thyroid abnormalities, and growth
Surgical repair of cleft palate or bifid uvula with associated feeding support
Metabolic medicine and clinical genetics referral with PGM1 testing and family counselling
